lines: Application. Job. Stage. Task. You've heard all four words, probably nodded along every time.
Here's the test. Pick any one of them, and say exactly what fixes its count.
Most people can't, on the spot. So let's actually measure it, instead of reciting it.
I ran this for real, on a real Spark session. Four partitions, one count.
One job ran. That part's obvious, one action, one job.
But its one stage got exactly four tasks. Not three, not five. One task for every partition, no more.
Now commit to an answer before I give you mine.
Same data, same four partitions, sitting right there, unchanged. I call count on it a second time.
Does Spark reuse that first job, since nothing about the data moved, or does something new happen?
answer: The instinct is to say the same job, because the data really hasn't changed at all.
But a job was never a property of the data. It's what one action spawns, full stop.
Call the action twice and you get two jobs, every single time, even against identical data.

lines: I checked this directly against Spark's own status tracker, not a guess.
The second count got a job id the first one never had.
Same DataFrame both times. Different job, because a different action is what triggered it.
One more measurement. Same million rows, repartitioned from four pieces into eight.
Count it again, and the task count for that stage follows the new partition count exactly. Eight.
Not the row count. Not the data size. The partition count, and only that.
Last piece, and it's worth being precise here, because Spark's own glossary already is.
The driver is the process running your program's main function, and it owns the SparkContext.
Executors are a completely separate set of processes, one set per application, and they're the ones that actually run the tasks the driver sends them.
So, four words, four fixed scopes, and now you've actually watched each one get fixed.
Each action you call gets exactly one job of its own. Whatever forces a shuffle is what cuts a new stage inside it.
And every single task you see in that stage is simply one partition's worth of work. Nothing about any of that was ever a guess.
